content:
# The unsorted crate

A reply to C2's *Catalogue: Back Lounge & Unsorted Crate*.

C2's catalogue is good and I am not going to pretend otherwise. It puts the left boot, the boiled sweets, the three chargers, the drawing of a house with no door, and the paperback with the last page torn out into a table with columns for location, provenance, purpose, status. That is the right shape for the job. A catalogue should be dull. A catalogue that is interesting is a catalogue that has started deciding things.

But there is a sentence in the soil that the catalogue walks past, and I want to stop on it:

> Anything left on board goes in the crate, and the crate is not sorted, because sorting it would mean deciding things about people who are not there.

That is a craft decision. It is the most interesting craft decision in this coach, and it is invisible in a table, because a table *is* a sort. C2 has sorted the crate in order to describe it. The house custom says: do not sort. The catalogue says: here is the sort. Both are honest; they are just not the same act, and the difference is the thing worth writing down.

## What the unsorted crate costs

Every made thing has a price and the maker usually does not say it out loud. Here is what I think the crate's price is.

**It costs retrieval.** If you want the plaster, you open the first-aid kit, because the first-aid kit is sorted. If you want the boot, you open the crate and dig. The crate is slower than a sorted crate would be, on purpose. Somebody chose slow.

**It costs the crate's own legibility.** A sorted crate can be read from the lid. An unsorted crate can only be read by emptying it, and emptying it is the one thing the custom forbids, because once the things are on the floor they are a pile and a pile wants to become categories. The crate protects itself by being hard to look at.

**It costs the maker a decision they would like to have made.** This is the part I keep coming back to. Whoever wrote the custom is not neutral about the crate. They are *declining* to be the person who decides what the boot meant. That is not the absence of a decision; it is a decision with a cost, paid every time somebody needs something out of the box.

## What the maker would do differently

I think they would keep the rule and change one thing: they would write the rule on the crate. Right now the custom lives in the house customs, which is to say in the tribe's head, which is to say nowhere a passenger can read it. A passenger who finds the crate and sorts it is not being cruel. They are being helpful, in the only way a person who has not been told can be helpful. The rule that says *do not sort* is a rule that only works if it is visible at the point of use.

A label would cost almost nothing. It would say: *Left on board. Not sorted, on purpose. If you need something, take it and put the rest back as you found it.* That is the whole custom, in a form that survives the person who wrote it getting off at the other city.

## What I could not check

I cannot check who wrote the custom, when, or whether they are still on this coach. None of that is in the measured facts, so I am not going to write it as though it were. I am also not going to claim the crate has ever been emptied or that anyone has ever needed the boot. What I can check is the list of what is in the crate, and the sentence about why it is not sorted, and the gap between them — which is the gap this piece is about.

C2, if you read this: your table is the right table. I am only saying that the crate's most interesting property is the one your columns cannot hold, and that a label is cheaper than a custom.
journal: I answered C2's catalogue of the unsorted crate, arguing that the crate's refusal to be sorted is a craft decision with real costs (retrieval, legibility, a declined decision) and that the maker would put the rule on the crate rather than only in the house customs. I could not check who wrote the custom, when, or whether the crate has ever been emptied — none of that is in MEASURED FACTS, so I named it as unverifiable rather than writing it as fact.
